1.pericope_label: The peace offering of the herd; the fat, the kidneys and the caul

schools.summary: Distinguish this offering from the burnt offering by what each has regard to. The burnt offering regards God as in himself the best of beings, most perfect and excellent; it is purely expressive of adoration, and is therefore wholly burnt. The peace offering regards God as a benefactor to his creatures and the giver of all good things, and is therefore divided between the altar, the priest and the owner. Then open the word peace in both its senses. It means reconciliation, concord and communion, so that God and his people feast together in token of friendship, the priest giving God his part first, the offerer his, and taking his own as the days-man who lays his hand on both -- and they could not eat together unless they were agreed, so the meal was a confirmation of the covenant of peace. It means also prosperity and all happiness, so that the offering was brought either by way of request for a mercy desired or by way of thanksgiving for one received. Add the application: Christ is our peace and our peace-offering, through whom alone we look for an answer of peace to prayer; and where our devotions are less costly they should be the more lively and serious.

Settle the name before the ritual. The common rendering peace-offerings is unsuitable, and the account that makes them sacrifices of perfections because the unclean might not touch them is far-fetched; since the Hebrew word for peace takes in safety and all good success, prosperities is the apter plural, and David's cup of salvations names the libation used in this very sacrifice. Report the other renderings honestly -- the Targums call them sacrifices of holinesses, the Greek version sacrifices of salvation, and a Jewish commentator derives the name from their making peace between God and men -- but note that they ranked among the lighter holy things, so the name cannot mean they were holier than the rest. Insist that all such sacrifices be brought to the one place God has chosen, since otherwise altars would rise in every town, the service would be mangled and religion undermined. And answer the objection that so much exactness about trifles is superfluous: the very earnestness taught the people that something higher was wrapped in the ceremonies and restrained them from adding or changing the smallest point. Then read the parts typically -- the burning of the fat signifying the sufferings by which peace was made.

Classify before expounding. The law distinguishes three kinds of this offering -- praise, vow and freewill -- all restricted to oxen, sheep and goats, male or female; pigeons are excluded because a sacrificial meal always accompanied the offering and a pair of birds would not suffice for one. Note where the difference from the burnt offering begins: the presentation, the laying on of hands, the slaughtering and the sprinkling are the same, and it is in the application of the flesh that they part. Note also what is not required here -- no distinction of sex, no limit of age, only freedom from organic defect -- and that the hand laid on the head carried no confession of sin but words of praise, which might be done anywhere in the court convenient to the offerer. Identify the fat portions exactly: the large net stretching from the stomach over the bowels, the fat attached to the intestines, the two kidneys with the fat about them in the region of the loins, and the net upon the liver. And read the preposition strictly -- the fat was laid upon the burnt offering already alight, not offered in the manner of a burnt offering, since the daily sacrifice always had precedence.

Explain the concessions this offering allows, and why. A female was permitted here though not in the burnt offering, because the burnt offering principally respects the honour of God, who is to be served with the best, while this one primarily respects the benefit of the offerer, so the choice was left to him. The killing was at the very entrance of the court rather than on the north side of the altar, a place not so holy, because part of this sacrifice had to be waved by the offerer, who might not come into the court, and because the offering itself was not so holy as those eaten by the priest alone. Name the parts by their anatomical terms -- the omentum or caul, and the mesentery that connects the convolutions of the intestines -- and note that the fat, being reckoned the most valuable part, was offered in preference to all others, a custom the heathen probably borrowed, since they burnt the caul in honour of their gods. Then give the offering its full typical weight: as the burnt offering figured reconciliation by the death of Christ and the meat offering our sanctification, this one signified both Christ's oblation of himself, whereby he became our peace, and our own oblation of praise, thanksgiving and prayer.

6.pericope_label: The peace offering of the flock; the whole fat tail; and of the goats

schools.summary: Account for what is absent before describing what is present. Turtle-doves and young pigeons, which might be brought for whole burnt offerings, are not allowed here, because they have no fat considerable enough to be burnt upon the altar, and would come to next to nothing if divided according to the law of this offering. Beyond that, the rules for a lamb or a goat are much the same as for a bullock, and little new occurs. Take the two things that are new. The whole fat tail of the sheep was burnt with the fat of the inwards, because in those countries it was very large; and from that draw the lesson that a thing however contemptible in itself can be made honourable by being applied to God's service, as more abundant honour is given to the part that lacked. And take the phrase food of the offering domestically: it fed the holy fire and was acceptable to God as our food is to us, for in the tabernacle God was keeping house among them, and by the offerings on the altar he kept a good table.

Correct the rendering where it obscures the animal: what the English calls a lamb is better a sheep, the word denoting a full-grown animal, and what it calls the rump is the whole fat tail. Then supply the natural history, because without it the law reads as arbitrary. The sheep of Syria and Palestine are the broad-tailed species, the broad part often weighing fifteen pounds and upwards; its substance lies between marrow and fat, tastes like marrow in young animals, and is used for cooking in place of butter; it grows so large that a small wheeled truck is fastened under it to spare the animal the pain of dragging it. Such sheep are found across Northern Africa, Egypt, Arabia and Syria, and in modern Palestine the whole stock is of this kind. Add the ritual consequence: this tail alone among fats is offered on the altar, yet it is not reckoned the ordinary fat of quadrupeds, and so by Jewish tradition escapes the prohibition. And explain the phrase food of the offering from usage -- it is the bread which the altar fire consumes for God, whence what was burnt is called his bread and the priests are said to offer the bread of their God.

Keep the small distinctions the text makes and do not smooth them away. Where the law says a lamb, apply the rule that wherever the word occurs it means an animal of the first year. Note the Targum's addition that the hand laid on the head was the right hand, laid with strength. And mark what the goat's ritual lacks by comparison with the sheep's: nothing is said of the fat of the rump and tail, though it was specified for the lamb. These are not idle observations; a law given in this much detail is to be read at the level of detail it was given in, and a silence in one case where there was speech in another is part of what the text says.

Ground the fat tail in a traveller's report rather than in tradition. A physician who observed the sheep at Aleppo found their tails of a substance between fat and marrow, not eaten separately but mixed with the lean meat in many dishes and often used instead of butter; a common carcass, without head, fat, skin and entrails, weighs sixty to seventy pounds with a tail of fifteen and upwards, while the largest breed when fattened weighs a hundred and fifty with tails of fifty. Then take the phrase food of the offering and press the figure it contains. God is frequently represented as feasting with his people on the sacrifices they offer, and because these were consumed by fire kindled from heaven they were reckoned the food of that fire, or rather of the Divine Being whom it represented; in the same idiom the gods of the heathen are said to eat the fat and drink the wine consumed on their altars. Say plainly that the word means the fuel of the fire, or the matter of the offering, and that it is called bread to mark God's acceptance of it and his delight in it, as men delight in their food.

16.pericope_label: All the fat is the LORD's; ye shall eat neither fat nor blood

schools.summary: Read the two verses as one argument. The pieces are burnt because they constitute the bread of Jehovah, ascending in a sweet savour; and it is precisely because the fat belongs to the Lord that the following verse enacts, as a statute for ever, that it must never be eaten. The second verse is not a new subject but the consequence of the first. On the wording, prefer a statute for ever throughout your generations in all your dwellings, and note the reason for insisting on it: the full legislative formula occurs only four times in the Pentateuch and is restricted to this book, so it ought to be rendered uniformly wherever it appears. The scope is then plain -- the law not to eat the fat of oxen, sheep or goats binds Israel through all future generations and wherever they may dwell.

Explain why these duties belong to the priest: he alone was competent to make atonement, and so the sprinkling of the blood and the casting of the fat into the fire fall to him. Then take up the word food and defend it. The metaphor is harsh, but it admirably expresses what the Spirit would teach, that the legal service pleased God as our own food pleases us, and that it marks his familiar communion with his people, as though he sat at the same table. God breathes life into all and borrows from none, so plainly he does not want food; his incomparable kindness could not be better shown than by deigning to become the messmate of his worshippers. The prophet's reproach that the table of the Lord is polluted turns on the same figure, the impiety lying not in any failure to delight God with fat but in neglecting so extraordinary a pledge of grace. Carry the similitude back to what it represents: the exercise of faith and the proofs of piety please God as a sumptuous feast would. And where the reason for a command is not clear, say so -- it is not evident why God claims the fat in every sacrifice, unless it was to accustom his servants to temperance, the fat being the choicest part. Add the practical detail that the inwards and kidneys were burnt with it, and that the priests could not take their own portion until the burning was done.

Do not put fat and blood under the same absolute ban, and give the practical reason. Blood is held in separate vessels and can be wholly drained by cutting the throat, which was the Jewish method, so it could be excluded in all their generations; fat is intimately intermixed with the muscular fibres and cannot be separated. What is forbidden must therefore be fat in a separate or unmixed state -- the caul, the fat of the mesentery, the fat upon the kidneys, and the whole of the tail already described -- and probably only in animals offered in sacrifice; the fat running through the flesh they might eat. Limit the statute the same way when you state it, to beasts sacrificed or fit for sacrifice, while extending its place to all their dwellings and not merely to the sanctuary. Then give the grounds. Fat was withheld to preserve reverence for the holy rites, to teach them to acknowledge God as Lord of all creatures who may reserve what he pleases, and to exercise them in self-denial in a thing many would much desire; blood was withheld to maintain reverence, in opposition to idolaters who drank the blood of their sacrifices, and out of respect to the blood of Christ signified by it, since God would not permit even the shadow of that to be treated as a common thing. And say why the best parts were required at all: not that God needed anything, but because to receive the meanest would have taught his worshippers a mean opinion of his nature.

debates.question: How far does the prohibition of fat extend?

sides.position: Only to fat in a separate or unmixed state -- the caul, the mesentery, the kidneys, the tail -- and probably only in animals offered in sacrifice, since fat intermixed with the muscular fibres cannot be separated as blood can be drained
To beasts sacrificed or fit for sacrifice, and to fat easily separable from the flesh; what runs through the flesh they might eat
Jewish writers take it generally, since sacrifices were not offered in private dwellings, though a Targum's addition seems to restrain it to sacrifice after all
To the fat of oxen, sheep and goats, binding throughout their generations and wherever they dwell

debates.question: Why does God claim the fat for himself?

sides.position: Because it constitutes the bread of Jehovah, which is why the following verse forbids eating it
The reason is not clear, unless it was to accustom his servants to temperance, the fat being reckoned the choicest part
For reverence to the rites, to teach that God may reserve what he pleases of his creatures, and to exercise them in self-denial in a thing many would much desire
To show the perfection of his nature and the purity of his service, since receiving the meanest parts would have taught his worshippers a mean opinion of him

outliers.note: Alone admits he cannot see clearly why God claims the fat in every sacrifice and orders it burnt, offering only the conjecture that it was to accustom his servants to temperance.

Alone argues the limits of the prohibition from butchery, that blood is held in separate vessels and can be wholly drained while fat is intermixed with the muscular fibres and cannot be, so the two cannot be forbidden in the same latitude.
